The '''atmosphere of Mars''' is the layer of gasses surrounding the planet [[Mars]]. It is primarily composed of [[carbon dioxide]] (95%), molecular [[nitrogen]] (2.85%), and [[argon]] (2%).<ref name="Franz-2017">{{Cite journal|last1=Franz|first1=Heather B.|last2=Trainer|first2=Melissa G.|last3=Malespin|first3=Charles A.|last4=Mahaffy|first4=Paul R.|last5=Atreya|first5=Sushil K.|last6=Becker|first6=Richard H.|last7=Benna|first7=Mehdi|last8=Conrad|first8=Pamela G.|last9=Eigenbrode|first9=Jennifer L.|date=2017-04-01|title=Initial SAM calibration gas experiments on Mars: Quadrupole mass spectrometer results and implications|journal=Planetary and Space Science|volume=138|pages=44–54|doi=10.1016/j.pss.2017.01.014|issn=0032-0633|bibcode=2017P&SS..138...44F}}</ref> It also contains trace levels of [[water vapor]], [[oxygen]], [[carbon monoxide]], [[hydrogen]], and [[noble gas]]es.<ref name="Haberle-2015">{{Citation|last=Haberle|first=R. M.|title=SOLAR SYSTEM/SUN, ATMOSPHERES, EVOLUTION OF ATMOSPHERES {{!}} Planetary Atmospheres: Mars|date=2015-01-01|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Atmospheric Sciences (Second Edition)|pages=168–177|editor-last=North|editor-first=Gerald R.|publisher=Academic Press|doi=10.1016/b978-0-12-382225-3.00312-1|isbn=978-0-12-382225-3|editor2-last=Pyle|editor2-first=John|editor3-last=Zhang|editor3-first=Fuqing}}</ref><ref name="Franz-2017"/><ref name="NSSDC-2021">{{Cite web|url=https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/marsfact.html|title=Mars Fact Sheet|website=nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov|access-date=2019-06-13|archive-date=23 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210823015113/https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/marsfact.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The [[atmosphere]] of Mars is much colder and thinner than [[Atmosphere of Earth|Earth's]], with an average temperature of {{convert|-59|C|F}},<ref name="NSSDC-2021" /> and a [[Atmospheric pressure|surface pressure]] of about {{convert|610|Pa}}, which is about 0.6% of the Earth's value.<ref name="Haberle-2015"/>

The density at the surface of Mars varies between about 10 and 20 g/m<sup>3</sup>, which is only 1–2% of Earth's value.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/marsfact.html|title=Mars Fact Sheet|access-date=17 January 2018|archive-date=23 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210823015113/https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/marsfact.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The density is about 25% lower during the southern winter than in spring and autumn because carbon dioxide freezes into a [[dry ice]] cap at the south pole,<ref name="Weather 2009">{{Cite web|title=Weather, Weather, Everywhere?|url=http://solarsystem.nasa.gov/scitech/display.cfm?ST_ID=725|access-date=2021-09-21|website=Solar System Exploration|archive-date=14 April 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090414055517/http://solarsystem.nasa.gov/scitech/display.cfm?ST_ID=725}}</ref><ref name="SeasonalCycles">{{cite web |title=Seasonal Cycles in Curiosity’s First Two Martian Years |url=https://science.nasa.gov/photojournal/seasonal-cycles-in-curiositys-first-two-martian-years/ |publisher=NASA |access-date=13 October 2026}}</ref> an effect that is smaller during the northern winter because of the highly eccentric [[orbit of Mars]].<ref name="Weather 2009" /> The low pressure of the Martian atmosphere prohibits the existence of liquid water on the [[Martian surface|surface of Mars]], but many studies suggest that the Martian atmosphere was much thicker in the past.<ref name="Catling-2017">{{Cite book|title=Atmospheric evolution on inhabited and F.|year=2017|isbn=978-0-521-84412-3|location=Cambridge|oclc=956434982|bibcode=2017aeil.book.....C}}</ref> The atmosphere of Mars has been losing mass to space since the planet's core slowed down, and the [[Atmospheric escape|leakage of gases]] continues today.<ref name="Catling-2017" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jakosky|first1=B. The atmosphere of Mars is colder than Earth's owing to the larger distance from the Sun, receiving less solar energy and has a lower [[effective temperature]], which is about {{Convert|210|K|C F}}.<ref name="Haberle-2015" /> The average surface emission temperature of Mars is just {{convert|215|K|C F}}, which is comparable to inland Antarctica.<ref name="Haberle-2015" /><ref name="Catling-2017" /> Although Mars's atmosphere consists primarily of carbon dioxide, the [[greenhouse effect]] in the Martian atmosphere is much weaker than Earth's: {{Convert|5|C-change|F-change}} on Mars, versus {{Convert|33|C-change|F-change}} on Earth due to the much lower density of carbon dioxide, leading to less greenhouse warming.<ref name="Haberle-2015" /><ref name="Catling-2017" /> Furthermore, the Martian atmosphere contains much less water vapor than Earth's atmosphere, and water vapor is another important contributor to the greenhouse effect. The daily range of temperature in the lower atmosphere presents ample variation due to the low thermal inertia; it can range from {{Convert|-75|C|F}} to near {{Convert|0|C|F}} near the surface in some regions.<ref name="Haberle-2015" /><ref name="Catling-2017" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://phys.org/news/2012-09-temperature-extremes-mars.html|title=Temperature extremes on Mars|website=phys.org|language=en-us|access-date=2019-06-13|archive-date=2 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201202005053/https://phys.org/news/2012-09-temperature-extremes-mars.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The temperature of the upper part of the Martian atmosphere is also significantly lower than Earth's because of the absence of [[Ozone layer|stratospheric ozone]] and the radiative cooling effect of carbon dioxide at higher altitudes.<ref name="Catling-2017" />

[[Dust devil]]s and [[dust storm]]s are prevalent on Mars, which are sometimes observable by telescopes from Earth,<ref name="Hille-2015">{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/feature/goddard/the-fact-and-fiction-of-martian-dust-storms|title=The Fact and Fiction of Martian Dust Storms|last=Hille|first=Karl|date=2015-09-18|website=NASA|access-date=2019-06-11|archive-date=2 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160302231423/http://www.nasa.gov/feature/goddard/the-fact-and-fiction-of-martian-dust-storms/|url-status=live}}</ref> and in 2018 even with the naked eye as a change in colour and brightness of the planet.<ref>https://skyandtelescope.org/astronomy-news/is-the-mars-opposition-already-over/[Normally reddish-orange or even pink, Mars now glows pumpkin-orange. Even my eyes can see the difference. ALPO assistant coordinator Richard Schmude has also noted an increase in brightness of ≈0.2 magnitude concurrent with the color change.]</ref> Planet-encircling dust storms (global dust storms) occur on average every 5.5 Earth years (every 3 Martian years) on Mars<ref name="Catling-2017"/><ref name="Hille-2015" /> and can threaten the operation of [[Mars rover]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/feature/jpl/opportunity-hunkers-down-during-dust-storm|title=Opportunity Hunkers Down During Dust Storm|last=Greicius|first=Tony|date=2018-06-08|website=NASA|access-date=2019-06-13|archive-date=30 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201130231214/https://www.nasa.gov/feature/jpl/opportunity-hunkers-down-during-dust-storm/|url-status=live}}</ref> However, the mechanism responsible for the development of large dust storms is still not well understood.<ref name="Kok-2012">{{Cite journal|last1=Kok|first1=Jasper F|last2=Parteli|first2=Eric J R|last3=Michaels|first3=Timothy I|last4=Karam|first4=Diana Bou|date=2012-09-14|title=The physics of wind-blown sand and dust|journal=Reports on Progress in Physics|volume=75|issue=10|article-number=106901|doi=10.1088/0034-4885/75/10/106901|pmid=22982806|issn=0034-4885|arxiv=1201.4353|bibcode=2012RPPh...75j6901K|s2cid=206021236}}</ref><ref name="Toigo 514–536">{{Cite journal|last1=Toigo|first1=Anthony D.|last2=Richardson|first2=Mark I.|last3=Wang|first3=Huiqun|last4=Guzewich|first4=Scott D.|last5=Newman|first5=Claire E.|date=2018-03-01|title=The cascade from local to global dust storms on Mars: Temporal and spatial thresholds on thermal and dynamical feedback|journal=Icarus|volume=302|pages=514–536|doi=10.1016/j.icarus.2017.11.032|issn=0019-1035|bibcode=2018Icar..302..514T}}</ref> It has been suggested to be loosely related to gravitational influence of [[Moons of Mars|both moons]], somewhat similar to the creation of [[tide]]s on Earth.

== Atmospheric evolution ==
{{See also|Atmospheric escape|Water on Mars}}The mass and composition of the Martian atmosphere are thought to have changed over the course of the planet's lifetime. A thicker, warmer and wetter atmosphere is required to explain several apparent features in the earlier history of Mars, such as the existence of liquid water bodies. Observations of the Martian upper atmosphere, measurements of isotopic composition and analyses of Martian meteorites, provide evidence of the long-term changes of the atmosphere and constraints for the relative importance of different processes.

In general, the gases found on modern Mars are depleted in lighter stable isotopes, indicating the Martian atmosphere has changed by some mass-selected processes over its history. Scientists often rely on these measurements of isotope composition to reconstruct conditions of the Martian atmosphere in the past.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/news.php?feature=4532 |title=Curiosity Sniffs Out History of Martian Atmosphere |website=NASA/JPL |access-date=2019-06-11 |archive-date=28 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200728150712/https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/news.php?feature=4532 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Nasa-2020">{{Cite web |url=https://mars.nasa.gov/news/1976/nasas-maven-reveals-most-of-mars-atmosphere-was-lost-to-space |title=NASA's MAVEN reveals most of Mars' atmosphere was lost to space |last=mars.nasa.gov |publisher=NASA's Mars Exploration Program |access-date=2019-06-11 |archive-date=17 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200817130320/https://mars.nasa.gov/news/1976/nasas-maven-reveals-most-of-mars-atmosphere-was-lost-to-space/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Catling200922">{{cite magazine |first1=David C. |last1=Catling |first2=Kevin J. |last2=Zahnle |url=http://faculty.washington.edu/dcatling/Catling2009_SciAm.pdf |title=The planetary air leak |magazine=[[Scientific American]] |date=May 2009 |page=26 |access-date=10 June 2019 |archive-date=26 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201026095634/http://faculty.washington.edu/dcatling/Catling2009_SciAm.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

While Mars and Earth have similar <sup>12</sup>C / [[carbon-13|<sup>13</sup>C]] and <sup>16</sup>O / [[oxygen-18|<sup>18</sup>O]] ratios, <sup>14</sup>N is much more depleted in the Martian atmosphere. It is thought that the photochemical escape processes are responsible for the [[Isotope fractionation|isotopic fractionation]] and has caused a significant loss of nitrogen on geological timescales.<ref name="Catling-2017"/> Estimates suggest that the initial [[partial pressure]] of N<sub>2</sub> may have been up to 30 hPa.<ref name="Av ice 20182"/><ref>{{cite journal |author1=McElroy, Michael B. |author2=Yung, Yuk Ling |author3=Nier, Alfred O. |s2cid=34066697 |date=1 October 1976 |title=Isotopic Composition of Nitrogen: Implications for the Past History of Mars' Atmosphere |journal=Science |volume=194 |issue=4260 |pages=70–72 |doi=10.1126/science.194.4260.70 |pmid=17793081 |bibcode=1976Sci...194...70M}}</ref>

[[Hydrodynamic escape]] in the early history of Mars may explain the isotopic fractionation of argon and xenon. On modern Mars, the atmosphere is not leaking these two [[noble gas]]es to outer space owing to their heavier mass. However, the higher abundance of hydrogen in the Martian atmosphere and the high fluxes of extreme UV from the young Sun, together could have driven a hydrodynamic outflow and dragged away these heavy gases.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hunten |first1=Donald M. |last2=Pepin |first2=Robert O. |last3=Walker |first3=James C.G. |date=1987-03-01 |title=Mass fractionation in hydrodynamic escape === Atmospheric escape on modern Mars ===
Despite the lower gravity, [[Atmospheric escape#Jeans escape|Jeans escape]] is not efficient in the modern Martian atmosphere due to the relatively low temperature at the exobase (≈200 K at 200 km altitude). It can only explain the escape of hydrogen from Mars. Other non-thermal processes are needed to explain the observed escape of oxygen, carbon and nitrogen.

==== Hydrogen escape ====
Molecular hydrogen (H<sub>2</sub>) is produced from the dissociation of H<sub>2</sub>O or other hydrogen-containing compounds in the lower atmosphere and diffuses to the exosphere. The exospheric H<sub>2</sub> then decomposes into hydrogen atoms, and the atoms that have sufficient thermal energy can escape from the gravitation of Mars (Jeans escape). The escape of atomic hydrogen is evident from the UV spectrometers on different orbiters.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Anderson|first=Donald E.|date=1974|title=Mariner 6, 7, and 9 Ultraviolet Spectrometer Experiment: Analysis of hydrogen Lyman alpha data|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research|volume=79|issue=10|pages=1513–1518|doi=10.1029/JA079i010p01513|issn=2156-2202|bibcode=1974JGR....79.1513A}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chaufray|first1=J.Y.|last2=Bertaux|first2=J.L.|last3=Leblanc|first3=F.|last4=Quémerais|first4=E.|date=June 2008|title=Observation of the hydrogen corona with SPICAM on Mars Express|journal=Icarus|volume=195|issue=2|pages=598–613|doi=10.1016/j.icarus.2008.01.009|bibcode=2008Icar..195..598C}}</ref> While most studies suggested that the escape of hydrogen is close to diffusion-limited on Mars,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hunten|first=Donald M.|date=November 1973|title=The Escape of Light Gases from Planetary Atmospheres|journal=Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences|volume=30|issue=8|pages=1481–1494|doi=10.1175/1520-0469(1973)030<1481:TEOLGF>2.0.CO;2|issn=0022-4928|bibcode=1973JAtS...30.1481H|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Zahnle|first1=Kevin|last2=Haberle|first2=Robert M.|last3=Catling|first3=David C.|last4=Kasting|first4=James F.|s2cid=2199349|date=2008|title=Photochemical instability of the ancient Martian atmosphere|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets|volume=113|issue=E11|pages=E11004|doi=10.1029/2008JE003160|issn=2156-2202|bibcode=2008JGRE..11311004Z|doi-access=free}}</ref> more recent studies suggest that the escape rate is modulated by dust storms and has a large seasonality.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bhattacharyya|first1=D.|last2=Clarke|first2=J. ==== Carbon escape ====
Photochemistry of CO<sub>2</sub> and CO in [[ionosphere]] can produce CO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> and CO<sup>+</sup> ions, respectively:

: {{chem2|CO2}} + {{mvar|hν}} ⟶ {{chem2|CO2+ + e-}}
: {{chem2|CO}} + {{mvar|hν}} ⟶ {{chem2|CO+ + e-}}

An ion and an electron can recombine and produce electronic-neutral products. The products gain extra kinetic energy due to the [[Coulomb's law|Coulomb attraction]] between ions and electrons. This process is called [[dissociative recombination]]. Dissociative recombination can produce carbon atoms that travel faster than the escape velocity of Mars, and those moving upward can then escape the Martian atmosphere:

: {{chem2|CO+ + e- ⟶ C + O}}
: {{chem2|CO2+ + e- ⟶ C + O2}}

UV photolysis of carbon monoxide is another crucial mechanism for the carbon escape on Mars:<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Nagy|first1=Andrew F.|last2=Liemohn|first2=Michael W.|last3=Fox|first3=J. L.|author-link3=Jane Lee Fox|last4=Kim|first4=Jhoon|date=2001|title=Hot carbon densities in the exosphere of Mars|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics|volume=106|issue=A10|pages=21565–21568|doi=10.1029/2001JA000007|issn=2156-2202|bibcode=2001JGR...10621565N|url=https://corescholar.libraries.wright.edu/physics/18|doi-access=free|access-date=24 November 2019|archive-date=28 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200728153549/https://corescholar.libraries.wright.edu/physics/18/|url-status=live}}</ref>

: {{chem2|CO}} + {{mvar|hν}} ({{mvar|λ}} < 116 nm) ⟶ {{chem2|C + O}}.

Other potentially important mechanisms include the [[Atmospheric escape#Non-thermal (suprathermal) escape|sputtering escape]] of CO<sub>2</sub> and collision of carbon with fast oxygen atoms.<ref name="Catling-2017" /> The estimated overall escape flux is about 0.6 × 10<sup>7</sup> cm<sup>−2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> to 2.2 × 10<sup>7</sup> cm<sup>−2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup> and depends heavily on solar activity.<ref name="Groller-2014">{{Cite journal|last1=Gröller|first1=H.|last2=Lichtenegger|first2=H.|last3=Lammer|first3=H.|last4=Shematovich|first4=V. I.|date=2014-08-01|title=Hot oxygen and carbon escape from the martian atmosphere|journal=Planetary and Space Science|series=Planetary evolution and life|volume=98|pages=93–105|doi=10.1016/j.pss.2014.01.007|issn=0032-0633|bibcode=2014P&SS...98...93G|arxiv=1911.01107|s2cid=122599784}}</ref><ref name="Catling-2017" />

==== Nitrogen escape ====
Like carbon, dissociative recombination of N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> is important for the nitrogen escape on Mars.<ref name="Fox-1993">{{Cite journal|last=Fox|first=J. Hartle|journal=Icarus|volume=192|issue=1|pages=296–301|doi=10.1016/j.icarus.2007.05.022|bibcode=2007Icar..192..296F}}</ref>

Nitrogen escape rate is very sensitive to the mass of the atom and solar activity. The overall estimated escape rate of <sup>14</sup>N is 4.8 × 10<sup>5</sup> cm<sup>−2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>.<ref name="Fox-1993" />

: {{chem2|CO2+ + O ⟶ O2+ + CO}}
: {{chem2|O2+ + e- ⟶ O + O}}

=== Ionospheric escape ===
The interaction of the [[solar wind]] and the [[interplanetary magnetic field]] with the Martian conductive ionosphere induces electrodynamic currents, that have been mapped and studied in detail, using MAVEN.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ramstad |first1=Robin |last2=Brain |first2=David A. |last3=Dong |first3=Yaxue |last4=Espley |first4=Jared |last5=Halekas |first5=Jasper |last6=Jakosky |first6=Bruce |date=October 2020 |title=The global current systems of the Martian induced magnetosphere |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41550-020-1099-y |journal=Nature Astronomy |language=en |volume=4 |issue=10 |pages=979–985 |doi=10.1038/s41550-020-1099-y |bibcode=2020NatAs...4..979R |issn=2397-3366|url-access=subscription }}</ref> These currents can drive the ionospheric species to high altitudes, where the solar wind is able to sweep them away from the planet, resulting to global scale ion outflows. They are however not sufficient to explain the atmospheric and ionospheric losses of Mars over its lifetime.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ramstad |first1=Robin |last2=Barabash |first2=Stas |last3=Futaana |first3=Yoshifumi |last4=Nilsson |first4=Hans |last5=Holmström |first5=Mats |date=November 2018 |title=Ion Escape From Mars Through Time: An Extrapolation of Atmospheric Loss Based on 10 Years of Mars Express Measurements |url=https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2018JE005727 |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets |language=en |volume=123 |issue=11 |pages=3051–3060 |doi=10.1029/2018JE005727 |bibcode=2018JGRE..123.3051R |issn=2169-9097|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Current chemical composition==
===Carbon dioxide===
{{See also|Martian polar ice caps|}}
CO<sub>2</sub> is the main component of the Martian atmosphere. It has a mean volume ([[molar concentration|molar]]) ratio of 94.9%.<ref name="Franz-2017"/> In winter polar regions, the surface temperature can be lower than the frost point of CO<sub>2.</sub> CO<sub>2</sub> gas in the atmosphere can condense on the surface to form 1–2 m thick solid [[dry ice]].<ref name="Catling-2017"/> In summer, the polar dry ice cap can undergo sublimation and release the CO<sub>2</sub> back to the atmosphere. As a result, significant annual variability in atmospheric pressure (≈25%) and atmospheric composition can be observed on Mars.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.msss.com/http/ps/seasons/seasons.html|title=Seasons on Mars|website=msss.com|access-date=2019-06-07|archive-date=3 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201103161520/https://www.msss.com/http/ps/seasons/seasons.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The condensation process can be approximated by the [[Clausius–Clapeyron relation]] for CO<sub>2</sub>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Soto |first1=Alejandro |last2=Mischna |first2=Michael |last3=Schneider |first3=Tapio |last4=Lee |first4=Christopher |last5=Richardson |first5=Mark |date=2015-04-01 |title=Martian atmospheric collapse: Idealized GCM studies |journal=Icarus |volume=250 |pages=553–569 |doi=10.1016/j.icarus.2014.11.028 |issn=0019-1035 |bibcode=2015Icar..250..553S |url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/53068/1/1-s2.0-S0019103514006575-main.pdf |access-date=30 August 2020 |archive-date=15 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170815231941/http://authors.library.caltech.edu/53068/1/1-s2.0-S0019103514006575-main.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Catling-2017" />

There also exists the potential for [[adsorption]] of CO<sub>2</sub> into and out of the [[regolith]] to contribute to the annual atmospheric variability. Despite the high concentration of CO<sub>2</sub> in the Martian atmosphere, the [[greenhouse effect]] is relatively weak on Mars (about 5 °C) because of the low concentration of water vapor and low atmospheric pressure. While water vapor in Earth's atmosphere has the largest contribution to greenhouse effect on modern Earth, it is present in only very low concentration in the Martian atmosphere. Moreover, under low atmospheric pressure, greenhouse gases cannot absorb infrared radiation effectively because the [[Pressure broadening|pressure-broadening]] effect is weak.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.esa.int/Our_Activities/Space_Science/Venus_Express/Greenhouse_effects_also_on_other_planets |title=Greenhouse effects ... also on other planets |publisher=[[European Space Agency]] |access-date=2019-06-07 |archive-date=29 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190929025950/http://www.esa.int/Our_Activities/Space_Science/Venus_Express/Greenhouse_effects_also_on_other_planets |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yung |first1=Yuk L. |last2=Kirschvink |first2=Joseph L. |last3=Pahlevan |first3=Kaveh |last4=Li |first4=King-Fai |date=2009-06-16 |title=Atmospheric pressure as a natural climate regulator for a terrestrial planet with a biosphere |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=106 |issue=24 |pages=9576–9579 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0809436106 |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=2701016 |pmid=19487662 |bibcode=2009PNAS..106.9576L|doi-access=free }}</ref>

In the presence of solar UV radiation (''hν'', photons with wavelength shorter than 225 nm), CO<sub>2</sub> in the Martian atmosphere can be [[photodissociation|photolyzed]] via the following reaction:

: {{chem2|CO2}} + {{mvar|hν}} ({{mvar|λ}} < 225 nm) ⟶ {{chem2|CO + O}}.

If there is no chemical production of CO<sub>2</sub>, all the CO<sub>2</sub> in the current Martian atmosphere would be removed by photolysis in about 3,500 years.<ref name="Catling-2017" /> The [[hydroxyl radical]]s (OH) produced from the photolysis of water vapor, together with the other odd hydrogen species (e.g. H, HO<sub>2</sub>), can convert carbon monoxide (CO) back to CO<sub>2</sub>. The reaction cycle can be described as:<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=McElroy |first1=M.B. |last2=Donahue |first2=T.M. |s2cid=30958948 |date=1972-09-15 |title=Stability of the Martian atmosphere |journal=Science |volume=177 |issue=4053 |pages=986–988 |doi=10.1126/science.177.4053.986 |pmid=17788809 |issn=0036-8075 |hdl=2060/19730010098 |hdl-access=free |bibcode=1972Sci...177..986M}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Parkinson |first1=T.D. |last2=Hunten|first2=D.M. |date=October 1972 |title=Spectroscopy and acronomy of O{{sub|2}} on Mars |journal=Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences |volume=29 |issue=7 |pages=1380–1390 |doi=10.1175/1520-0469(1972)029<1380:SAAOOO>2.0.CO;2 |issn=0022-4928 |bibcode=1972JAtS...29.1380P |doi-access=free}}</ref>

: {{chem2|CO + OH ⟶ CO2 + H}}
: {{chem2|H + O2 + M ⟶ HO2 + M}}
: {{chem2|HO2 + O ⟶ OH + O2}}
: {{chem2|Net: CO + O ⟶ CO2}}

Mixing also plays a role in regenerating CO<sub>2</sub> by bringing the O, CO, and O<sub>2</sub> in the upper atmosphere downward.<ref name="Catling-2017" /> The balance between photolysis and redox production keeps the average concentration of CO<sub>2</sub> stable in the modern Martian atmosphere.

CO<sub>2</sub> ice clouds can form in winter polar regions and [[cirrus clouds|at very high altitudes]] (>50 km) in tropical regions, where the air temperature is lower than the frost point of CO<sub>2</sub>.<ref name="Haberle-2015"/><ref name="Stevens-2017">{{Cite journal|last1=Stevens |first1=M.H. |last2=Siskind|first2=D.E. |last3=Evans |first3=J.S. |last4=Jain |first4=S.K. |last5=Schneider |first5=N.M. |last6=Deighan |first6=J. |last7=Stewart |first7=A.I.F. |last8=Crismani |first8=M. |last9=Stiepen |first9=A. |date=2017-05-28 |title=Martian mesospheric cloud observations by IUVS on MAVEN: Thermal tides coupled to the upper atmosphere: IUVS Martian Mesospheric Clouds |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |volume=44 |issue=10 |pages=4709–4715 |doi=10.1002/2017GL072717 |hdl=10150/624978 |s2cid=13748950 |hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Gonzalez-Galindo-2011">{{Cite journal |last1=González-Galindo |first1=Francisco |last2=Määttänen |first2=Anni |last3=Forget |first3=François |last4=Spiga |first4=Aymeric |date=2011-11-01 |title=The martian mesosphere as revealed by CO{{sub|2}} cloud observations and general circulation modeling |journal=Icarus |volume=216 |issue=1 |pages=10–22 |doi=10.1016/j.icarus.2011.08.006 |issn=0019-1035 |bibcode=2011Icar..216...10G}}</ref>

===Nitrogen===
N<sub>2</sub> is the second most abundant gas in the Martian atmosphere. It has a mean volume ratio of 2.6%.<ref name="Franz-2017" /> Various measurements showed that the Martian atmosphere is enriched in [[Isotopes of nitrogen#Nitrogen-15|<sup>15</sup>N]].<ref name="Jakosky 20153">{{cite journal |last1=Stevens |first1=M.H. |last2=Evans |first2=J.S. |last3=Schneider |first3= N.M. |last4=Stewart |first4=A.I.F. |last5=Deighan |first5=J. |last6=Jain |first6=S.K. |last7=Crismani |first7=M. |last8=Stiepen |first8=A. |last9=Chaffin |first9=M.S. |last10=McClintock |first10=W.E. |last11=Holsclaw |first11=G.M. |last12=Lefèvre |first12=F. |last13=Lo |first13=D.Y. |last14=Clarke |first14=J.T. |last15=Montmessin |first15=F. |last16=Bougher |first16=S.W. |last17=Jakosky |first17=B.M. |year=2015 |title=New observations of molecular nitrogen in the Martian upper atmosphere by IUVS on MAVEN |journal=Geophysical Research Letters |volume=42 |issue=21 |pages=9050–9056 |doi=10.1002/2015GL065319 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2015GeoRL..42.9050S}}</ref><ref name="Av ice 20182">{{cite journal |last1=Avice |first1=G. |last2=Bekaert |first2=D.V. |last3=Chennaoui Aoudjehane |first3=H. |author3-link=Hasnaa Chennaoui Aoudjehane|last4=Marty |first4=B. |date=9 February 2018 |title=Noble gases and nitrogen in Tissint reveal the composition of the Mars atmosphere |journal=Geochemical Perspectives Letters |volume=6 |pages=11–16 |doi=10.7185/geochemlet.1802 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The enrichment of heavy isotopes of nitrogen is possibly caused by mass-selective escape processes.<ref name="Mandt 20153">{{cite journal |author1=Mandt, Kathleen |author2=Mousis, Olivier |author3=Chassefière, Eric |date=1 July 2015 |title=Comparative planetology of the history of nitrogen isotopes in the atmospheres of Titan and Mars |journal=Icarus |volume=254 |pages=259–261 |doi=10.1016/j.icarus.2015.03.025 |pmc=6527424 |pmid=31118538 |bibcode=2015Icar..254..259M}}</ref>

===Argon===
Argon is the third most abundant gas in the Martian atmosphere. It has a mean volume ratio of 1.9%.<ref name="Franz-2017"/> In terms of stable isotopes, Mars is enriched in <sup>38</sup>Ar relative to <sup>36</sup>Ar, which can be attributed to hydrodynamic escape.

One of [[Isotopes of argon|Argon's isotopes]], <sup>40</sup>Ar, is produced from the [[radioactive decay]] of <sup>40</sup>K. In contrast, <sup>36</sup>Ar is primordial: It was present in the atmosphere after the formation of Mars. Observations indicate that Mars is enriched in <sup>40</sup>Ar relative to <sup>36</sup>Ar, which cannot be attributed to mass-selective loss processes.<ref name="Mahaffy-2013">{{Cite journal |last1=Mahaffy |first1=P.R. |last2=Webster |first2=C.R. |last3=Atreya |first3=S.K. |last4=Franz |first4=H. |last5=Wong |first5=M. |last6=Conrad |first6=P.G. |last7=Harpold |first7=D. |last8=Jones |first8=J.J. |last9=Leshin |first9=L.A. |date=2013-07-19 |title=Abundance and isotopic composition of gases in the Martian atmosphere from the Curiosity rover |journal=Science |volume=341 |issue=6143 |pages=263–266 |issn=0036-8075 |doi=10.1126/science.1237966 |pmid=23869014 |bibcode=2013Sci...341..263M |s2cid=206548973}}</ref> A possible explanation for the enrichment is that a significant amount of primordial atmosphere, including <sup>36</sup>Ar, was lost by impact erosion in the early history of Mars, while <sup>40</sup>Ar was emitted to the atmosphere after the impact.<ref name="Mahaffy-2013"/><ref name="Catling-2017"/>

===Oxygen and ozone===
The estimated mean volume ratio of molecular oxygen (O<sub>2</sub>) in the Martian atmosphere is 0.174%.<ref name="Franz-2017"/> It is one of the products of the photolysis of CO<sub>2</sub>, water vapor, and [[ozone]] (O{{sub|3}}). It can react with atomic oxygen (O) to re-form ozone (O{{sub|3}}). In 2010, the [[Herschel Space Observatory]] detected molecular oxygen in the Martian atmosphere.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hartogh |first1=P. |last2=Jarchow |first2=C. |last3=Lellouch |first3=E. |last4=de Val-Borro |first4=M. |last5=Rengel |first5=M. |last6=Moreno |first6=R. |last7=Medvedev |first7=A.S. |last8=Sagawa |first8=H. |last9=Swinyard |first9=B.M. |last10=Cavalié |first10=T. |last11=Lis |first11=D.C. |last12=Błęcka |first12=M.I. |last13=Banaszkiewicz |first13=M. |last14=Bockelée-Morvan |first14=D. |last15=Crovisier |first15=J. |last16=Encrenaz |first16=T.|author16-link=Thérèse Encrenaz |last17=Küppers |first17=M. |last18=Lara |first18=L.-M. |last19=Szutowicz |first19=S. |last20=van den Bussche |first20=B. |last21=Bensch |first21=F. |last22=Bergin |first22=E.A. |last23=Billebaud |first23=F. |last24=Biver |first24=N. |last25=Blake |first25=G.A. |last26=Blommaert |first26=J.A.D.L. |last27=Cernicharo |first27=J. |last28=Decin |first28=L. |last29=Encrenaz |first29=P.|author29-link=Thérèse Encrenaz |last30=Feuchtgruber |first30=H. |display-authors=6 |year=2010 |title=Herschel / HIFI observations of Mars: First detection of O{{sub|2}} at sub-millimetre wavelengths and upper limits on HCL and H{{sub|2}}O{{sub|2}} |url=https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2010/13/aa15160-10/aa15160-10.html |journal=Astronomy and Astrophysics |volume=521 |pages=L49 |doi=10.1051/0004-6361/201015160  |doi-access=free|bibcode=2010A&A...521L..49H |arxiv=1007.1301 |s2cid=119271891 |access-date=6 February 2019 |archive-date=7 February 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190207015254/https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2010/13/aa15160-10/aa15160-10.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Atomic oxygen is produced by photolysis of CO<sub>2</sub> in the upper atmosphere and can escape the atmosphere via dissociative recombination or ion pickup. In early 2016, [[Stratospheric Observatory for Infrared Astronomy|Stratospheric Observatory for Infrared Astronomy (SOFIA)]] detected [[atomic oxygen]] in the atmosphere of Mars, which has not been found since the Viking and Mariner mission in the 1970s.<ref name="nasa.gov3">{{Cite web |url=https://www.nasa.gov/feature/ames/sofia/flying-observatory-detects-atomic-oxygen-in-martian-atmosphere |title=Flying Observatory Detects Atomic Oxygen in Martian Atmosphere – NASA<!-- Bot generated title --> |date=6 May 2016 |access-date=18 March 2017 |archive-date=8 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201108101219/https://www.nasa.gov/feature/ames/sofia/flying-observatory-detects-atomic-oxygen-in-martian-atmosphere/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2019, NASA scientists working on the ''Curiosity'' rover mission, who have been taking measurements of the gas, discovered that the amount of oxygen in the Martian atmosphere rose by 30% in spring and summer.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-50419917|title=Nasa probes oxygen mystery on Mars|date=14 November 2019|publisher=BBC News|access-date=15 November 2019|archive-date=17 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200117183603/https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-50419917|url-status=live}}</ref>

Similar to stratospheric ozone in Earth's atmosphere, the ozone present in the Martian atmosphere can be destroyed by catalytic cycles involving odd hydrogen species:

: {{chem2|H + O3 ⟶ OH + O2}}
: {{chem2|O + OH ⟶ H + O2}}
: Net: {{chem2|O + O3 ⟶  2O2}}

Since water is an important source of these odd hydrogen species, higher abundance of ozone is usually observed in the regions with lower water vapor content.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Krasnopolsky|first=Vladimir A.|date=2006-11-01|title=Photochemistry of the martian atmosphere: Seasonal, latitudinal, and diurnal variations|journal=Icarus|volume=185|issue=1|pages=153–170|doi=10.1016/j.icarus.2006.06.003|issn=0019-1035|bibcode=2006Icar..185..153K}}</ref> Measurements showed that the total column of ozone can reach 2–30 μm-atm around the poles in winter and spring, where the air is cold and has low water saturation ratio.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Perrier |first1=S. |last2=Bertaux |first2=J.L. |last3=Lefèvre |first3=F. |last4=Lebonnois |first4=S. |last5=Korablev|first5=O. |last6=Fedorova |first6=A. |last7=Montmessin |first7=F. |year=2006 |title=Global distribution of total ozone on Mars from SPICAM/MEX UV measurements|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research |series=Planets |volume=111 |issue=E9 |pages=E09S06 |doi=10.1029/2006JE002681 |issn=2156-2202 |bibcode=2006JGRE..111.9S06P |doi-access=free}}</ref> The actual reactions between ozone and odd hydrogen species may be further complicated by the heterogeneous reactions that take place in water-ice clouds.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Perrier |first1=Séverine |last2=Montmessin |first2=Franck |last3=Lebonnois |first3=Sébastien |last4=Forget |first4=François |last5=Fast |first5=Kelly |last6=Encrenaz |first6=Thérèse|author6-link=Thérèse Encrenaz |last7=Clancy|first7=R. It is thought that the vertical distribution and seasonality of ozone in the Martian atmosphere is driven by the complex interactions between chemistry and transport of oxygen-rich air from sunlit latitudes to the poles.<ref name="Montmessin-2013">{{cite journal |last1=Franck Lefèvre |last2=Montmessin |first2=Franck |date=November 2013 |title=Transport-driven formation of a polar ozone layer on Mars |journal=Nature Geoscience |volume=6 |issue=11 |pages=930–933 |doi=10.1038/ngeo1957 |issn=1752-0908 |bibcode=2013NatGe...6..930M}}</ref><ref name="ESA-2019">{{cite web |url=http://sci.esa.int/mars-express/52881-a-seasonal-ozone-layer-over-the-martian-south-pole/ |title=A seasonal ozone layer over the Martian south pole |series=[[Mars Express]] |publisher=[[European Space Agency]] |website=sci.esa.int |access-date=2019-06-03 |archive-date=3 June 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190603213141/http://sci.esa.int/mars-express/52881-a-seasonal-ozone-layer-over-the-martian-south-pole/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The UV/IR [[spectrometer]] on ''[[Mars Express]]'' (SPICAM) has shown the presence of two distinct ozone layers at low-to-mid latitudes. These comprise a persistent, near-surface layer below an altitude of {{Convert|30|km|mi|abbr=on}}, a separate layer that is only present in northern spring and summer with an altitude varying from 30 to 60 km, and another separate layer that exists 40–60 km above the southern pole in winter, with no counterpart above the Mars's north pole.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lebonnois |first1=Sébastien |last2=Quémerais |first2=Eric |last3=Montmessin |first3=Franck |last4=Lefèvre |first4=Franck |last5=Perrier |first5=Séverine |last6=Bertaux |first6=Jean-Loup |last7=Forget |first7=François |s2cid=55162288 |year=2006 |title=Vertical distribution of ozone on Mars as measured by SPICAM/Mars Express using stellar occultations |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research |series=Planets |volume=111 |issue=E9 |pages=E09S05 |doi=10.1029/2005JE002643 |issn=2156-2202 |bibcode=2006JGRE..111.9S05L |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00109865/file/8fb300f315ff537a95f0f59c8d42b449f415.pdf |doi-access=free |access-date=30 August 2020 |archive-date=8 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201108170342/https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00109865/file/8fb300f315ff537a95f0f59c8d42b449f415.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> This third ozone layer shows an abrupt decrease in elevation between 75 and 50 degrees south. SPICAM detected a gradual increase in ozone concentration at {{Convert|50|km|mi|abbr=on}} until midwinter, after which it slowly decreased to very low concentrations, with no layer detectable above {{Convert|35|km|mi|abbr=on}}.<ref name="Montmessin-2013"/>

=== Sulfur dioxide ===
[[Sulfur dioxide]] (SO<sub>2</sub>) in the atmosphere would be an indicator of current volcanic activity. It has become especially interesting due to the long-standing controversy of methane on Mars. === Other trace gases ===
Carbon monoxide (CO) is produced by the photolysis of CO<sub>2</sub> and quickly reacts with the oxidants in the Martian atmosphere to re-form CO<sub>2</sub>. The estimated mean volume ratio of CO in the Martian atmosphere is 0.0747%.<ref name="Franz-2017" />

== Vertical structure ==
[[File:Mars annotated-vertical-profiles.png|thumb|400x400px|The vertical structure of the atmosphere of Mars overlying with temperature profiles retrieved from the entry probes of Mars landers. Data source: NASA Planetary Data System|alt=]]
The vertical temperature structure of the Martian atmosphere differs from Earth's atmosphere in many ways. Information about the vertical structure is usually inferred by using the observations from thermal infrared [[Atmospheric sounding|soundings]], [[radio occultation]], [[aerobraking]], landers' entry profiles.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Smith|first=Michael D.|s2cid=102489157|date=May 2008|title=Spacecraft Observations of the Martian Atmosphere|journal=Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences|volume=36|issue=1|pages=191–219|doi=10.1146/annurev.earth.36.031207.124334|issn=0084-6597|bibcode=2008AREPS..36..191S}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Withers|first1=Paul|last2=Catling|first2=D. C.|s2cid=26311417|date=December 2010|title=Observations of atmospheric tides on Mars at the season and latitude of the Phoenix atmospheric entry|journal=Geophysical Research Letters|volume=37|issue=24|article-number=2010GL045382 |pages=n/a|doi=10.1029/2010GL045382|bibcode=2010GeoRL..3724204W|doi-access=free}}</ref> Mars's atmosphere can be classified into three layers according to the average temperature profile:
* Troposphere (≈0–40 km): The layer where most of the weather phenomena (e.g. convection and dust storms) take place. Its dynamics is heavily driven by the daytime surface heating and the amount of suspended dust. Mars has a higher [[scale height]] of 11.1 km than Earth (8.5 km) because of its weaker gravity.<ref name="NSSDC-2021"/> The theoretical dry adiabatic [[lapse rate]] of Mars is 4.3 °C km<sup>−1</sup>,<ref name="Leovy-2001">{{Cite journal|last=Leovy|first=Conway|date=July 2001|title=Weather and climate on Mars|journal=Nature|volume=412|issue=6843|pages=245–249|doi=10.1038/35084192|pmid=11449286|bibcode=2001Natur.412..245L|s2cid=4383943|issn=1476-4687}}</ref> but the measured average lapse rate is about 2.5 °C km<sup>−1</sup> because the suspended dust particles absorb solar radiation and heat the air.<ref name="Haberle-2015" /> The [[planetary boundary layer]] can extend to over 10 km thick during the daytime.<ref name="Haberle-2015" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Petrosyan|first1=A.|last2=Galperin|first2=B.|last3=Larsen|first3=S. E.|last4=Lewis|first4=S. R.|last5=Määttänen|first5=A.|last6=Read|first6=P. L.|last7=Renno|first7=N.|last8=Rogberg|first8=L. P. H. T.|last9=Savijärvi|first9=H.|date=2011-09-17|journal=Reviews of Geophysics|volume=49|issue=3|pages=RG3005|doi=10.1029/2010RG000351|issn=8755-1209|bibcode=2011RvGeo..49.3005P|title=The Martian Atmospheric Boundary Layer|hdl=2027.42/94893|s2cid=37493454|hdl-access=free}}</ref> The near-surface diurnal temperature range is huge (60 °C<ref name="Leovy-2001" />) due to the low thermal inertia. Under dusty conditions, the suspended dust particles can reduce the surface diurnal temperature range to only 5 °C.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Atmospheric evolution on inhabited and lifeless worlds|last=Catling|first=David C.|date=13 April 2017|others=Kasting, James F.|isbn=978-0-521-84412-3|location=Cambridge|oclc=956434982|bibcode=2017aeil.book.....C}}</ref> The temperature above 15 km is controlled by radiative processes instead of convection.<ref name="Haberle-2015" /> Mars is also a rare exception to the "0.1-bar tropopause" rule found in the other atmospheres in our solar system.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Robinson|first1=T. D.|last2=Catling|first2=D. C.|date=January 2014|title=Common 0.1 bar tropopause in thick atmospheres set by pressure-dependent infrared transparency|journal=Nature Geoscience|volume=7|issue=1|pages=12–15|arxiv=1312.6859|doi=10.1038/ngeo2020|issn=1752-0894|bibcode=2014NatGe...7...12R|s2cid=73657868}}</ref>
* Mesosphere (≈40–100 km): The layer that has the lowest temperature. CO<sub>2</sub> in the mesosphere acts as a cooling agent by efficiently radiating heat into space. Stellar occultation observations show that the [[mesopause]] of Mars locates at about 100 km (around 0.01 to 0.001 Pa level) and has a temperature of 100–120 K.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Forget|first1=François|last2=Montmessin|first2=Franck|last3=Bertaux|first3=Jean-Loup|last4=González-Galindo|first4=Francisco|last5=Lebonnois|first5=Sébastien|last6=Quémerais|first6=Eric|last7=Reberac|first7=Aurélie|last8=Dimarellis|first8=Emmanuel|last9=López-Valverde|first9=Miguel A.|date=2009-01-28|title=Density and temperatures of the upper Martian atmosphere measured by stellar occultations with Mars Express SPICAM|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research|volume=114|issue=E1|pages=E01004|doi=10.1029/2008JE003086|issn=0148-0227|url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00357038/file/Forget_et_al-2009-Journal_of_Geophysical_Research__Solid_Earth_%281978-2012%29.pdf|bibcode=2009JGRE..114.1004F|s2cid=2660831 |access-date=24 June 2019|archive-date=3 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190503133316/https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00357038/file/Forget_et_al-2009-Journal_of_Geophysical_Research__Solid_Earth_%281978-2012%29.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> The temperature can sometimes be lower than the frost point of CO<sub>2</sub>, and detections of CO<sub>2</sub> ice clouds in the Martian mesosphere have been reported.<ref name="Stevens-2017"/><ref name="Gonzalez-Galindo-2011"/>
* Thermosphere (≈100–230 km): The layer is mainly controlled by [[Extreme ultraviolet|extreme UV]] heating. The temperature of the Martian thermosphere increases with altitude and varies by season. The daytime temperature of the upper thermosphere ranges from 175 K (at aphelion) to 240 K (at perihelion) and can reach up to 390 K,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bougher|first1=S. W.|last2=Pawlowski|first2=D.|last3=Bell|first3=J. M.|last4=Nelli|first4=S.|last5=McDunn|first5=T.|last6=Murphy|first6=J. R.|last7=Chizek|first7=M.|last8=Ridley|first8=A.|date=February 2015|title=Mars Global Ionosphere-Thermosphere Model: Solar cycle, seasonal, and diurnal variations of the Mars upper atmosphere: BOUGHER ET AL.|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets|volume=120|issue=2|pages=311–342|doi=10.1002/2014JE004715|hdl=2027.42/110830|s2cid=91178752|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bougher|first1=Stephen W.|last2=Roeten|first2=Kali J.|last3=Olsen|first3=Kirk|last4=Mahaffy|first4=Paul R.|last5=Benna|first5=Mehdi|last6=Elrod|first6=Meredith|last7=Jain|first7=Sonal K.|last8=Schneider|first8=Nicholas M.|last9=Deighan|first9=Justin|date=2017|title=The structure and variability of Mars dayside thermosphere from MAVEN NGIMS and IUVS measurements: Seasonal and solar activity trends in scale heights and temperatures|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics|volume=122|issue=1|pages=1296–1313|doi=10.1002/2016JA023454|issn=2169-9402|bibcode=2017JGRA..122.1296B|doi-access=free|hdl=2027.42/136242|hdl-access=free}}</ref> but it is still significantly lower than the temperature of [[Thermosphere|Earth's thermosphere]]. The higher concentration of CO<sub>2</sub> in the Martian thermosphere may explain part of the discrepancy because of the cooling effects of CO<sub>2</sub> in high altitude. It is thought that [[aurora]]l heating processes is not important in the Martian thermosphere because of the absence of a strong magnetic field in Mars, but the [[MAVEN]] orbiter has detected several aurora events.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/image-feature/goddard/maven-captures-aurora-on-mars|title=MAVEN Captures Aurora on Mars|last=Zell|first=Holly|date=2015-05-29|website=NASA|access-date=2019-06-05|archive-date=31 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200731174049/https://www.nasa.gov/image-feature/goddard/maven-captures-aurora-on-mars/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nasa.gov/feature/jpl/large-solar-storm-sparks-global-aurora-and-doubles-radiation-levels-on-the-martian-surface|title=NASA Missions See Effects at Mars From Large Solar Storm|last=Greicius|first=Tony|date=2017-09-28|website=NASA|access-date=2019-06-05|archive-date=8 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190608041335/https://www.nasa.gov/feature/jpl/large-solar-storm-sparks-global-aurora-and-doubles-radiation-levels-on-the-martian-surface/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Mars does not have a persistent stratosphere due to the lack of shortwave-absorbing species in its middle atmosphere (e.g. [[Ozone layer|stratospheric ozone]] in Earth's atmosphere and organic haze in [[Atmosphere of Jupiter|Jupiter's atmosphere]]) for creating a temperature inversion.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://marsed.asu.edu/mep/atmosphere|title=Mars Education {{!}} Developing the Next Generation of Explorers|website=marsed.asu.edu|access-date=2019-06-03|archive-date=3 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190603213152/https://marsed.asu.edu/mep/atmosphere|url-status=live}}</ref> However, a seasonal ozone layer and a strong temperature inversion in the middle atmosphere have been observed over the Martian south pole.<ref name="ESA-2019" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=McCleese|first1=D. J.|last2=Schofield|first2=J. T.|last3=Taylor|first3=F. W.|last4=Abdou|first4=W. A.|last5=Aharonson|first5=O.|last6=Banfield|first6=D.|last7=Calcutt|first7=S. B.|last8=Heavens|first8=N. == Atmospheric dust and other dynamic features ==
=== Atmospheric dust ===
{{See also|mineral dust|Martian soil#Atmospheric dust}}Under sufficiently strong wind (> 30 m/s), dust particles can be mobilized and lifted from the surface to the atmosphere.<ref name="Haberle-2015" /><ref name="Catling-2017" /> Some of the dust particles can be suspended in the atmosphere and travel by circulation before falling back to the ground.<ref name="Kok-2012"/> Dust particles can attenuate solar radiation and interact with infrared radiation, which can lead to a significant radiative effect on Mars. ==== Dust storms ====
{{Further|Climate of Mars#Dust storms|Dust storms#On Mars}}
[[File:2005-1103mars-full.jpg|thumb|Difference of dust and water clouds: the orange cloud at the center of the image is a large dust cloud, the other white polar clouds are water clouds.]]
[[File:Dust storm co.tif|thumb|right|Detail of a Martian dust storm, as viewed from orbit]]
[[File:Dust clouds over Mars ESA384856.jpg|thumb|right|A 700 kilometer long dust storm front (marked by the red arrow) as viewed from orbit at different angles. The red circle of Martian terrain is just for orientation.]]
[[File:PIA03170 fig1duststroms.jpg|thumb|Mars without a dust storm in June 2001 (on left) and with a global dust storm in July 2001 (on right), as seen by Mars Global Surveyor]]

Local and regional dust storms are not rare on Mars.<ref name="Kok-2012" /><ref name="Haberle-2015" /> Local storms have a size of about 10<sup>3</sup> km<sup>2</sup> and occurrence of about 2000 events per Martian year, while regional storms of 10<sup>6</sup> km<sup>2</sup> large are observed frequently in southern spring and summer.<ref name="Haberle-2015" /> Near the polar cap, dust storms sometimes can be generated by frontal activities and extra-tropical cyclones.<ref name="Read-2015">{{Cite journal|last1=Read|first1=P L|last2=Lewis|first2=S R|last3=Mulholland|first3=D P|date=2015-11-04|title=The physics of Martian weather and climate: a review|journal=Reports on Progress in Physics|volume=78|issue=12|article-number=125901|doi=10.1088/0034-4885/78/12/125901|pmid=26534887|issn=0034-4885|url=http://oro.open.ac.uk/44802/1/__userdata_documents9_srl89_Desktop_readlewismulholland2015iop.pdf|bibcode=2015RPPh...78l5901R|s2cid=20087052 |access-date=24 June 2019|archive-date=20 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180720203925/http://oro.open.ac.uk/44802/1/__userdata_documents9_srl89_Desktop_readlewismulholland2015iop.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Kok-2012" />

Global dust storms (area > 10<sup>6</sup> km<sup>2</sup> ) occur on average once every 3 Martian years.<ref name="Catling-2017" /> Observations showed that larger dust storms are usually the result of merging smaller dust storms,<ref name="Hille-2015"/><ref name="Toigo 514–536"/> but the growth mechanism of the storm and the role of atmospheric feedbacks are still not well understood.<ref name="Toigo 514–536" /><ref name="Kok-2012" /> Although it is thought that Martian dust can be entrained into the atmosphere by processes similar to Earth's (e.g. [[Saltation (geology)|saltation]]), the actual mechanisms are yet to be verified, and electrostatic or magnetic forces may also play in modulating dust emission.<ref name="Kok-2012" /> Researchers reported that the largest single source of [[Martian soil#Atmospheric dust|dust]] on Mars comes from the [[Medusae Fossae Formation]].<ref name="NC-20180720">{{cite journal|last1=Ojha|first1=Lujendra|last2=Lewis|first2=Kevin|last3=Karunatillake|first3=Suniti|last4=Schmidt|first4=Mariek|date=20 July 2018|title=The Medusae Fossae Formation as the single largest source of dust on Mars|journal=[[Nature Communications]]|volume=9|page=2867|number=2867 (2018)|bibcode=2018NatCo...9.2867O|doi=10.1038/s41467-018-05291-5|doi-access=free|pmid=30030425|pmc=6054634}}</ref>

==== Dust devils ====
{{Main|Martian dust devils}}
[[File:PIA24039-MarsCuriosityRover-DustDevil-20200809.gif|thumb|center|700px|<div align="center">A small [[dust devil]] on Mars – viewed by the ''[[Curiosity (rover)|Curiosity]]'' rover – (9 August 2020)</div>]]
Dust devils are common on Mars.<ref name="Whelley 2008">{{Cite journal|last1=Whelley|first1=Patrick L.|last2=Greeley|first2=Ronald|date=2008|title=The distribution of dust devil activity on Mars|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets|volume=113|issue=E7|pages=E07002|doi=10.1029/2007JE002966|issn=2156-2202|bibcode=2008JGRE..113.7002W|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Kok-2012" /> Like their counterparts on Earth, dust devils form when the convective vortices driven by strong surface heating are loaded with dust particles.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Balme|first1=Matt|last2=Greeley|first2=Ronald|s2cid=53391259|date=2006|title=Dust devils on Earth and Mars|journal=Reviews of Geophysics|volume=44|issue=3|pages=RG3003|doi=10.1029/2005RG000188|issn=1944-9208|bibcode=2006RvGeo..44.3003B|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Nasa-2018">{{Cite web|url=https://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2005/14jul_dustdevils|title=The Devils of Mars {{!}} Science Mission Directorate|website=science.nasa.gov|access-date=2019-06-11|archive-date=26 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181226011822/https://science.nasa.gov/science-news/science-at-nasa/2005/14jul_dustdevils/|url-status=live}}</ref> Dust devils on Mars usually have a diameter of tens of meters and height of several kilometers, which are much taller than the ones observed on Earth.<ref name="Haberle-2015" /><ref name="Nasa-2018" /> Study of dust devils' tracks showed that most of Martian dust devils occur at around 60°N and 60°S in spring and summer.<ref name="Whelley 2008" /> They lift about 2.3 × 10<sup>11</sup> kg of dust from land surface to atmosphere annually, which is comparable to the contribution from local and regional dust storms.<ref name="Whelley 2008" />

==== Wind modification of the surface ====
On Mars, the near-surface wind is not only emitting dust but also modifying the geomorphology of Mars over long time scales. Although it was thought that the atmosphere of Mars is too thin for mobilizing the sandy features, observations made by [[High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment|HiRISE]] showed that the migration of dunes is not rare on Mars.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://uanews.arizona.edu/story/mars-sands-shift-different-drum|title=On Mars, Sands Shift to a Different Drum|last1=Stolte|first1=Daniel|last2=Communications|first2=University|website=UANews|date=22 May 2019|access-date=2019-06-11|archive-date=4 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190604060840/https://uanews.arizona.edu/story/mars-sands-shift-different-drum|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/MRO/news/mro20111117.html|title=NASA – NASA Orbiter Catches Mars Sand Dunes in Motion|website=nasa.gov|access-date=2019-06-11|archive-date=26 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200726125903/https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/MRO/news/mro20111117.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Urso 427–430">{{Cite journal|last1=Urso|first1=Anna C.|last2=Fenton|first2=Lori K.|last3=Banks|first3=Maria E.|last4=Chojnacki|first4=Matthew|date=2019-05-01|title=Boundary condition controls on the high-sand-flux regions of Mars|journal=Geology|volume=47|issue=5|pages=427–430|doi=10.1130/G45793.1|pmid=32440031|pmc=7241575|issn=0091-7613|bibcode=2019Geo....47..427C|doi-access=free}}</ref> The global average migration rate of dunes (2 – 120 m tall) is about 0.5 meter per year.<ref name="Urso 427–430" /> Atmospheric circulation models suggested repeated cycles of wind erosion and dust deposition can lead, possibly, to a net transport of soil materials from the lowlands to the uplands on geological timescales.<ref name="Catling-2017" />
[[File:Ripple Movement on Sand Dune in Nili Patera, Mars.gif|center|thumb|Movement of sandy features in [[Nili Patera dune field]] on Mars detected by HiRISE. Photo credit: NASA/JPL Caltech/U. Arizona/JHU-APL|alt=]]

=== Thermal tides ===
{{See also|Atmospheric tide}}Solar heating on the day side and radiative cooling on the night side of a planet can induce pressure difference.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Thermal_tide|title=Thermal tide – AMS Glossary|website=glossary.ametsoc.org|access-date=2019-06-11|archive-date=26 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200726110400/http://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Thermal_tide|url-status=live}}</ref> Thermal tides, which are the wind circulation and waves driven by such a daily-varying pressure field, can explain a lot of variability of the Martian atmosphere.<ref name="Lee-2009">{{Cite journal|last1=Lee|first1=C.|last2=Lawson|first2=W. G.|last3=Richardson|first3=M. I.|last4=Heavens|first4=N. G.|last5=Kleinböhl|first5=A.|last6=Banfield|first6=D.|last7=McCleese|first7=D. J.|last8=Zurek|first8=R.|last9=Kass|first9=D.|date=2009|title=Thermal tides in the Martian middle atmosphere as seen by the Mars Climate Sounder|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets|volume=114|issue=E3|pages=E03005|doi=10.1029/2008JE003285|issn=2156-2202|pmc=5018996|pmid=27630378|bibcode=2009JGRE..114.3005L}}</ref> Compared to Earth's atmosphere, thermal tides have a larger influence on the Martian atmosphere because of the stronger diurnal temperature contrast.<ref name="Kieffer-1992" /> The surface pressure measured by Mars rovers showed clear signals of thermal tides, although the variation also depends on the shape of the planet's surface and the amount of suspended dust in the atmosphere.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/msl/multimedia/pia16478.html|title=NASA – Thermal Tides at Mars|website=nasa.gov|access-date=2019-06-11|archive-date=17 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190617061606/https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/msl/multimedia/pia16478.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The atmospheric waves can also travel vertically and affect the temperature and water-ice content in the middle atmosphere of Mars.<ref name="Lee-2009" />

=== Orographic clouds ===
{{See also|Orographic lift#Associated clouds}}
[[File:Arsia Mons Cloud - Mars Express - Flickr - jccwrt.png|thumb|Water-ice clouds formed in the vicinity of the [[Arsia Mons]] volcano. The image was taken on 21 September 2018, but similar cloud formation events had been observed in the same site before. Photo credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin|alt=]]
On Earth, mountain ranges sometimes force an air mass to rise and cool down. As a result, water vapor becomes saturated and clouds are formed during the lifting process.<ref>{{Cite web| url=http://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Orographic_cloud|title=Orographic cloud – AMS Glossary| website=glossary.ametsoc.org|access-date=2019-06-11|archive-date=10 September 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190910204942/http://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Orographic_cloud|url-status=live}}</ref> On Mars, orbiters have observed a seasonally recurrent formation of huge water-ice clouds around the downwind side of the 20 km-high volcanoes [[Arsia Mons]], which is likely caused by the same mechanism.<ref>{{Cite web| url=http://www.esa.int/Our_Activities/Space_Science/Mars_Express/Mars_Express_keeps_an_eye_on_curious_cloud|title=Mars Express keeps an eye on curious cloud|last=esa|website=European Space Agency| access-date=2019-06-11|archive-date=15 June 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190615064628/https://www.esa.int/Our_Activities/Space_Science/Mars_Express/Mars_Express_keeps_an_eye_on_curious_cloud|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web| url=http://redplanet.asu.edu/?p=31294|title=Mars Express: Keeping an eye on a curious cloud {{!}} Red Planet Report|last=rburnham|access-date=2019-06-11|archive-date=27 September 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190927014051/http://redplanet.asu.edu/?p=31294|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Acoustic environment ==
[[File:NASA-SoundsOnMars-PerseveranceRover-20220401.webm|thumb|right|200px|<div align="center">Mars sounds ([[Perseverance (rover)|''Perseverance'']]) (video; 1:29; 1 April 2022)</div>]]
In April 2022, scientists reported, for the first time, studies of [[Sound#Waves|sound waves]] on Mars. These studies were based on measurements by instruments on the [[Perseverance (rover)|''Perseverance'' rover]]. The scientists found that the [[speed of sound]] is slower in the thin Martian atmosphere than on Earth. The speed of sound on Mars, within the [[Hearing range|audible bandwidth]] between 20 Hz – 20 kHz, varies depending on [[Audio frequency|pitch]], seemingly due to the low pressure and thermal turbulence of Martian surface air; and, as a result of these conditions, sound is much quieter, and live music would be more variable, than on Earth.<ref name="NAT-20220401">{{cite journal |author=Maurice, S |title=In situ recording of Mars soundscape |date=1 April 2022 |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=605 |issue=7911 |pages=653–658 |doi=10.1038/s41586-022-04679-0 |pmid=35364602 |pmc=9132769 |bibcode=2022Natur.605..653M |s2cid=247865804 }}</ref><ref name="NASA-20220401">{{cite news |last1=Agle |first1=DC |last2=Fox |first2=Karen |last3=Johnson |first3=Alana |last4=Brennan |first4=Pat |title=What Sounds Captured by NASA's Perseverance Rover Reveal About Mars – A new study based on recordings made by the rover finds that the speed of sound is slower on the Red Planet than on Earth and that, mostly, a deep silence prevails. |url=https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/what-sounds-captured-by-nasas-perseverance-rover-reveal-about-mars |date=1 April 2022 |work=[[NASA]] |access-date=5 April 2022 }}</ref><ref name="VICE-20220404">{{cite news |last=Ferreira |first=Becky |title=Sound on Mars Has a 'Unique' And Extremely Trippy Property, Recordings Reveal – Mars has two speeds of sound, which "may induce a unique listening experience on Mars with an early arrival of high-pitched sounds compared to bass. |url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/sound-on-mars-has-a-unique-and-extremely-trippy-property-recordings-reveal/ |date=4 April 2022 |work=[[Vice (magazine)|Vice]] |access-date=5 April 2022 }}</ref>

== Unexplained phenomena ==

=== Detection of methane ===
{{Main|Methane on Mars}}[[Methane]] (CH<sub>4</sub>) is chemically unstable in the current oxidizing atmosphere of Mars. It would quickly break down due to ultraviolet radiation from the Sun and chemical reactions with other gases. Therefore, a persistent presence of methane in the atmosphere may imply the existence of a source to continually replenish the gas.

The [[Trace Gas Orbiter|ESA-Roscosmos Trace Gas Orbiter]], which has made the most sensitive measurements of methane in Mars's atmosphere with over 100 global [[Atmospheric sounding|soundings]], has found no methane to a detection limit of 0.05 [[parts per billion]] (ppb).<ref name="Vago-2019" /><ref name="First results 2019" /><ref name="Weule-2019" /> However, there have been other reports of detection of methane by ground-based telescopes and the ''Curiosity'' rover. Trace amounts of methane, at the level of several ppb, were first reported in Mars's atmosphere by a team at the NASA [[Goddard Space Flight Center]] in 2003.<ref name="methane33">{{cite journal|author1=Mumma, M. J.|author2=Novak, R. E.|author3=DiSanti, M. A.|author4=Bonev, B. P.|year=2003|title=A Sensitive Search for Methane on Mars|journal=Bulletin of the American Astronomical Society|volume=35|page=937|bibcode=2003DPS....35.1418M}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.skyandtelescope.com/astronomy-news/mars-methane-boosts-chances-for-life/|title=Mars Methane Boosts Chances for Life|author=Naeye, Robert|date=28 September 2004|work=[[Sky & Telescope]]|access-date=20 December 2014|archive-date=20 December 2014|archive-url=https://archive.today/20141220141048/http://www.skyandtelescope.com/astronomy-news/mars-methane-boosts-chances-for-life/|url-status=live}}</ref> Large differences in the abundances were measured between observations taken in 2003 and 2006, which suggested that the methane was locally concentrated and probably seasonal.<ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1126/science.359.6371.16 | volume=359 | title=Mars methane rises and falls with the seasons | year=2018 | journal=Science | pages=16–17 | last1 = Hand | first1 = Eric| issue=6371 | pmid=29301992 | bibcode=2018Sci...359...16H }}</ref>

In 2014, NASA reported that the ''Curiosity'' rover detected a tenfold increase ('spike') in methane in the atmosphere around it in late 2013 and early 2014. Four measurements taken over two months in this period averaged 7.2 ppb, implying that Mars is episodically producing or releasing methane from an unknown source.<ref name="Webster-2015">{{Cite journal|last1=Webster|first1=C. ===Super-rotating jet over the equator===
Super-rotation refers to the phenomenon that atmospheric mass has a higher angular velocity than the surface of the planet at the equator, which in principle cannot be driven by inviscid axisymmetric circulations.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Laraia|first1=Anne L.|last2=Schneider|first2=Tapio|date=2015-07-30|title=Superrotation in Terrestrial Atmospheres|journal=Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences|volume=72|issue=11|pages=4281–4296|doi=10.1175/JAS-D-15-0030.1|issn=0022-4928|url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/62447/1/jas-d-15-0030.1.pdf|bibcode=2015JAtS...72.4281L|s2cid=30893675 |access-date=24 June 2019|archive-date=23 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180723173830/https://authors.library.caltech.edu/62447/1/jas-d-15-0030.1.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Read 175–202">{{Cite journal|last1=Read|first1=Peter L.|last2=Lebonnois|first2=Sebastien|date=2018-05-30|title=Superrotation on Venus, on Titan, and Elsewhere|journal=Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences|volume=46|issue=1|pages=175–202|doi=10.1146/annurev-earth-082517-010137|issn=0084-6597|bibcode=2018AREPS..46..175R|s2cid=134203070|doi-access=free}}</ref> Assimilated data and general circulation model (GCM) simulation suggest that super-rotating jet can be found in Martian atmosphere during global dust storms, but it is much weaker than the ones observed on slow-rotating planets like Venus and Titan.<ref name="Read-2015"/> GCM experiments showed that the thermal tides can play a role in inducing the super-rotating jet.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lewis|first1=Stephen R.|last2=Read|first2=Peter L.|date=2003|title=Equatorial jets in the dusty Martian atmosphere|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets|volume=108|issue=E4|page=5034|doi=10.1029/2002JE001933|issn=2156-2202|bibcode=2003JGRE..108.5034L|url=http://oro.open.ac.uk/4896/1/lewisread2003.pdf|access-date=30 July 2019|archive-date=26 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200726110940/http://oro.open.ac.uk/4896/1/lewisread2003.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> Nevertheless, modeling super-rotation still remains as a challenging topic for planetary scientists.<ref name="Read 175–202"/>

==History of atmospheric observations==
{{Main|History of Mars observation}}
[[File:PIA16800-MarsCuriosityRover-MtSharp-ColorVersions-20120823.jpg|thumb|right|300px|Comparison of color versions (raw, natural, white balance) of [[Mount Sharp|Mount Sharp (Aeolis Mons)]], illustrating the [[Extraterrestrial skies#Mars|color of and lighting conditions on Mars and its atmosphere]].]]

In 1784, German-born British astronomer [[William Herschel]] published an article about his observations of the Martian atmosphere in ''[[Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society]]'' and noted the occasional movement of a brighter region on Mars, which he attributed to clouds and vapors.<ref name="Kieffer-1992">{{Cite book|title=Mars|date=1992|publisher=University of Arizona Press|last=Kieffer|first=Hugh H.|isbn=0-8165-1257-4|location=Tucson|oclc=25713423|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/mars0000unse}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Herschel William|s2cid=186212257|date=1784-01-01|title=XIX. On the remarkable appearances at the polar regions of the planet Mars, and its spheroidical figure; with a few hints relating to its real diameter and atmosphere.|journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London|volume=74|pages=233–273|doi=10.1098/rstl.1784.0020}}</ref> In 1809, French astronomer [[Honoré Flaugergues]] wrote about his observation of "yellow clouds" on Mars, which are likely to be dust storm events.<ref name="Kieffer-1992" /> In 1864, [[William Rutter Dawes]] observed that "the ruddy tint of the planet does not arise from any peculiarity of its atmosphere; it seems to be fully proved by the fact that the redness is always deepest near the centre, where the atmosphere is thinnest."<ref name="dawes">{{cite journal|last=Dawes|first=W.R.|year=1865|title=Physical Observations of Mars Near the Opposition in 1864|journal=Astronomical Register|volume=3|pages=220.1|bibcode=1865AReg....3..220D}}</ref> Spectroscopic observations in the 1860s and 1870s<ref name="campbell2">{{cite journal|last=Campbell|first=W.W.|year=1894|title=Concerning an Atmosphere on Mars|journal=Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific|volume=6|issue=38|page=273|bibcode=1894PASP....6..273C|doi=10.1086/120876|doi-access=free}}</ref> led many to think the atmosphere of Mars is similar to Earth's. In 1894, though, [[Spectroscopy|spectral analysis]] and other qualitative observations by [[William Wallace Campbell]] suggested Mars resembles the [[Moon]], which has no appreciable atmosphere, in many respects.<ref name="campbell2" /> In 1926, photographic observations by [[William Hammond Wright]] at the [[Lick Observatory]] allowed [[Donald Howard Menzel]] to discover quantitative evidence of Mars's atmosphere.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Wright|first=W. H.|year=1925|title=Photographs of Mars made with light of different colors|journal=Lick Observatory Bulletin|volume=12|pages=48–61|doi=10.5479/ADS/bib/1925LicOB.12.48W|bibcode=1925LicOB..12...48W}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Menzel|first=D. H.|year=1926|title=The Atmosphere of Mars|journal=The Astrophysical Journal|volume=61|page=48|bibcode=1926ApJ....63...48M|doi=10.1086/142949|doi-access=free}}</ref>

With an enhanced understanding of optical properties of atmospheric gases and advancement in [[spectrometer]] technology, scientists started to measure the composition of the Martian atmosphere in the mid-20th century. Lewis David Kaplan and his team detected the signals of water vapor and carbon dioxide in the spectrogram of Mars in 1964,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kaplan|first1=Lewis D.|last2=Münch|first2=Guido|last3=Spinrad|first3=Hyron|date=January 1964|title=An Analysis of the Spectrum of Mars.|journal=The Astrophysical Journal|volume=139|page=1|doi=10.1086/147736|issn=0004-637X|bibcode=1964ApJ...139....1K|url=https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechAUTHORS:20150811-124650209}}</ref> as well as carbon monoxide in 1969.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kaplan|first1=Lewis D.|last2=Connes|first2=J.|last3=Connes|first3=P.|date=September 1969|title=Carbon Monoxide in the Martian Atmosphere|journal=The Astrophysical Journal|volume=157|pages=L187|doi=10.1086/180416|issn=0004-637X|bibcode=1969ApJ...157L.187K|doi-access=free}}</ref> In 1965, the measurements made during [[Mariner 4|Mariner 4']]s flyby confirmed that the Martian atmosphere is constituted mostly of carbon dioxide, and the surface pressure is about 400 to 700 Pa.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/news.php?feature=5469|title=Mariner 4 Anniversary Marks 30 Years of Mars Exploration|website=NASA/JPL|access-date=2019-06-09|archive-date=28 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200728163910/https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/news.php?feature=5469|url-status=live}}</ref> After the composition of the Martian atmosphere was known, [[Astrobiology|astrobiological]] research began on Earth to determine the viability of [[life on Mars]]. Containers that simulated environmental conditions on Mars, called "[[Mars jar]]s", were developed for this purpose.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Scoles|first=Sarah|date=2020-07-24|title=The Doctor From Nazi Germany and the Roots of the Hunt for Life on Mars|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/07/24/science/mars-jars-strughold.html|access-date=2020-07-24|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=25 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201125035837/https://www.nytimes.com/2020/07/24/science/mars-jars-strughold.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 1976, two landers of the [[Viking program]] provided the first ever in-situ measurements of the composition of the Martian atmosphere. Another objective of the mission included investigations for evidence of past or present life on Mars (see [[Viking lander biological experiments]]).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kemppinen |first1=O |last2=Tillman |first2=J.E |last3=Schmidt |first3=W |last4=Harri |first4=A.-M |title=New analysis software for Viking Lander meteorological data |journal= Geoscientific Instrumentation, Methods and Data Systems|date=2013 |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=61–69 |doi=10.5194/gi-2-61-2013 |bibcode=2013GI......2...61K |doi-access=free }}</ref> Since then, many orbiters and landers have been sent to Mars to measure different properties of the Martian atmosphere, such as concentration of trace gases and isotopic ratios. In addition, telescopic observations and analysis of [[Martian meteorite]]s provide independent sources of information to verify the findings. The imageries and measurements made by these spacecraft greatly improve our understanding of the atmospheric processes outside Earth. The rover ''[[Curiosity (rover)|Curiosity]]'' and the lander ''[[InSight]]'' are still operating on the surface of Mars to carry out experiments and report the local daily weather.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://mars.nasa.gov/insight/weather|title=Mars Weather at Elysium Planitia|last=mars.nasa.gov|website=NASA's InSight Mars Lander|date=4 December 2017 |language=en|access-date=2019-06-13|archive-date=1 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201201001449/https://mars.nasa.gov/insight/weather/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://mars.nasa.gov/msl/mission/instruments/environsensors/rems/|title=Rover Environmental Monitoring Station (REMS) – NASA Mars Curiosity Rover|last=NASA|first=JPL|website=mars.nasa.gov|date=30 November 2017 |access-date=2019-06-13|archive-date=12 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112035630/https://mars.nasa.gov/msl/spacecraft/instruments/rems/|url-status=live}}</ref> The rover ''[[Perseverance (rover)|Perseverance]]'' and helicopter ''[[Ingenuity (helicopter)|Ingenuity]]'', which formed the [[Mars 2020]] program, landed in February 2021. The rover ''[[Rosalind Franklin (rover)|Rosalind Franklin]]'' is scheduled to launch in 2028.

==Potential for use by humans==
{{Main|In-situ resource utilization|Terraforming of Mars|Colonization of Mars}}
The atmosphere of Mars is a resource of known composition available at any landing site on Mars. It has been proposed that [[human mission to Mars|human exploration of Mars]] could use [[carbon dioxide]] (CO<sub>2</sub>) from the Martian atmosphere to make methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) and use it as [[rocket fuel]] for the return mission. Mission studies that propose using the atmosphere in this way include the [[Mars Direct]] proposal of [[Robert Zubrin]] and the NASA [[Design Reference Mission]] study. Two major chemical pathways for use of the carbon dioxide are the [[Sabatier reaction]], converting atmospheric carbon dioxide along with additional hydrogen (H<sub>2</sub>) to produce methane (CH<sub>4</sub>) and oxygen (O<sub>2</sub>), and [[electrolysis]], using a [[zirconia]] solid oxide electrolyte to split the carbon dioxide into oxygen (O<sub>2</sub>) and carbon monoxide (CO).<ref>{{Cite web|title=NASA Wants to Make Rocket Fuel From Martian Soil – ExtremeTech|url=https://www.extremetech.com/extreme/279947-nasa-wants-to-make-rocket-fuel-from-martian-soil|access-date=2020-09-23|website=extremetech.com|date=November 2018 |archive-date=26 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200926080131/https://www.extremetech.com/extreme/279947-nasa-wants-to-make-rocket-fuel-from-martian-soil|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2021, the NASA rover ''[[Perseverance (rover)|Perseverance]]'' was able to make oxygen on Mars. The process is complex and takes a lot of time to produce a small amount of oxygen.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.fox29.com/news/nasas-perseverance-rover-produces-oxygen-on-mars-in-historic-first-water-could-be-next-scientists-say | title=NASA's Perseverance rover produces oxygen on Mars in historic first – water could be next, scientists say | date=22 April 2021 }}</ref> As of 2023, it had produced a total of 122 grams of oxygen and was able to produce 12 grams per hour.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nasa.gov/missions/mars-2020-perseverance/perseverance-rover/nasas-oxygen-generating-experiment-moxie-completes-mars-mission/ | title=NASA's Oxygen-Generating Experiment MOXIE Completes Mars Mission – NASA | date=6 September 2023 }}</ref> Martian air passes through a HEPA filter, is compressed and heated to 800 °C, and is then sent to a nickel-based cathode where the carbon dioxide is decomposed into oxygen ions and CO. A scandia-stabilized zirconia ceramic electrolyte then sorts and passes oxygen ions to the anode, where the oxygen ions recombine into O<sub>2</sub>.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1126/sciadv.abp8636 | title=Mars Oxygen ISRU Experiment (MOXIE)—Preparing for human Mars exploration | date=2022 | last1=Hoffman | first1=Jeffrey A. | last2=Hecht | first2=Michael H. | last3=Rapp | first3=Donald | last4=Hartvigsen | first4=Joseph J. | last5=Soohoo | first5=Jason G. | last6=Aboobaker | first6=Asad M. | last7=McClean | first7=John B. | last8=Liu | first8=Andrew M. | last9=Hinterman | first9=Eric D. | last10=Nasr | first10=Maya | last11=Hariharan | first11=Shravan | last12=Horn | first12=Kyle J. | last13=Meyen | first13=Forrest E. | last14=Okkels | first14=Harald | last15=Steen | first15=Parker | last16=Elangovan | first16=Singaravelu | last17=Graves | first17=Christopher R. | last18=Khopkar | first18=Piyush | last19=Madsen | first19=Morten B. | last20=Voecks | first20=Gerald E. | last21=Smith | first21=Peter H. | last22=Skafte | first22=Theis L. | last23=Araghi | first23=Koorosh R. | last24=Eisenman | first24=David J. | journal=Science Advances | volume=8 | issue=35 | article-number=eabp8636 | pmid=36044563 | bibcode=2022SciA....8P8636H | pmc=9432831 }}</ref>
